property_summary: The proxiableUUID function must return ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT for UUPS compatibility; the buggy version returns a different constant, violating the required return value.
The function proxiableUUID must return ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT to satisfy the UUPS standard; the buggy version returns a different constant, so the return values differ.
The proxiableUUID function must return the ERC1967 implementation slot constant; the buggy version returns a hardcoded 0xDEADBEEF instead, so any call will return a different value.

The function proxiableUUID must return the value defined in ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the buggy version returns a different constant, so the return values will differ for any non-delegated call.

For the reference contract, proxiableUUID() always returns the standard IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT bytes32 (0x3608...bbbc). The buggy version instead returns ADMIN_SLOT (0xb531...6103), so the two return values differ for any call that does not revert.

The function proxiableUUID() must return IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT (0x360894a13ba1a3210667c828492db98dca3e2076cc3735a920a3ca505d382bbc); the buggy version returns BEACON_SLOT instead, violating the ERC-7201 UUPS standard and the contract's self-identification invariant.
For any notDelegated call, proxiableUUID must return ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the mutant returns BEACON_SLOT, violating the UUPS identification invariant.

The proxiableUUID function must return the ERC1967 implementation slot bytes32(0x360894a13ba1a3210667c828492db98dca3e2076cc3735a920a3ca505d382bbc) for any non-delegated call; the mutant returns bytes32(0) instead.
For any non-delegated call, proxiableUUID() must return the ERC1967 implementation slot; the mutant returns bytes32(0), violating the invariant for all such calls.
The function proxiableUUID must return the correct ERC1967 implementation slot for any call, but the mutant returns a different hash constant.
For any valid caller, c.proxiableUUID() must return the constant ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT, but the mutant returns an unpredictable address-dependent value.
The proxiableUUID function must return the constant ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT for all calls, but the mutant returns a block.timestamp-dependent value that changes on every call.

After initialization, the reference contract correctly reports its UUPS upgradeable interface version as '5.0.0', but the mutant fails to initialize UUPS state, so calling upgradeToAndCall will revert with UUPSUnauthorizedCallContext instead of succeeding.

After initialization, the reference contract correctly identifies itself as a UUPS proxy returning the canonical implementation slot, while the mutant fails to properly set up UUPS state, causing proxiableUUID to revert due to the notDelegated modifier checking address(this) != __self.
After initialization, calling proxiableUUID() on the reference contract succeeds and returns the canonical implementation slot, while on the mutant it reverts due to uninitialized UUPS state.
After initialization, calling upgradeToAndCall on the reference contract with a valid implementation succeeds without reverting, while the mutant reverts due to uninitialized UUPS proxy state.

After initialize, calling proxiableUUID() on reference returns IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT without revert, but the mutant's proxiableUUID() reverts because the UUPS state is uninitialized, breaking the invariant that a correctly initialized contract should successfully report its proxiable UUID.

After initialization, the access control storage is set to a non-zero address in the reference contract, whereas in the mutant it remains the zero address, so calling a function with an access check via the same msgsender will revert in the reference and succeed in the mutant.

After calling initialize(x), any subsequent call to a checkAccess-protected function (like setSlopes) from an unauthorized account must revert due to the access control being set; in the mutant, such calls succeed because access control is never configured.

After initialize, calling any access-controlled function (e.g., setSlopes) from any address must revert in the reference because access was initialized, but in the mutant it succeeds because access was never set.

After calling initialize(address) with any non-zero address, a subsequent call to setSlopes from a non-owner EOA must revert due to missing access rights; in the mutant, the call succeeds because access control is never set.

After initialization, calling the access-controlled function setSlopes() from any external address must revert due to uninitialized access control, whereas in the mutant the call succeeds because access was never set.
After initialization, the access control of C is never address(0) in the reference, but the mutant sets it to address(0), allowing any caller to use access-controlled functions like setSlopes.

After initialization, the access control storage of C must be non-zero for the reference, but the mutant sets it to zero, which can be observed via a revert on a subsequent call to setSlopes that would succeed only when access control is properly configured.

After initialize is called, the access control address must be non-zero in the reference, but the mutant sets it to zero, which causes any access-controlled function (such as setSlopes) to always revert when called by a non-zero caller, whereas the reference would succeed for an authorized caller.

After initialize, a call to setSlopes with valid parameters by any non-zero caller must succeed in the reference (since the caller is an accessControl admin) but must revert in the mutant (since accessControl is zero, which always denies access).

After initialization, a subsequent call to setSlopes by any address must not revert in the reference if access control is set to that address, but always reverts in the mutant because access control is zero, denying all access.

After initialize, the access control address set by __Access_init must match the expected access control; swapping calls leaves _accessControl unset (zero) because __UUPSUpgradeable_init doesn't set it, violating the invariant that initialize correctly stores the access control.

After initialize, calling any access-controlled function (e.g., setLimits) with the correct admin must succeed via checkAccess; the reordered init leaves accessControl unset (zero), so checkAccess reverts even for the rightful admin.

After initialize, the caller that performed initialization (address(this) in the test context) is the access control admin, and calling setLimits with that admin via a pranked call must succeed (not revert); the reordered init fails to store the admin, so setLimits reverts for the same admin.
After initialization, the stored access control address must equal the address passed to initialize(); the reordered init leaves it as zero, breaking the rule.
After initialize, a call to setSlopes with the correct access control caller must not revert; the bug leaves accessControl zero, so even an admin-pranked call reverts.

After initialization, the public getter for _initialized should return exactly 1 for the correct contract, but the mutant mistakenly sets it to 2, causing a second call to the initializer to succeed when it should revert.
After a successful `initialize`, the contract is permanently initialized; any subsequent call to `initialize` must revert, for any admissible sender.

The reference initializer sets _initialized to 1 and emits Initialized(1), while the mutant sets _initialized to 2 but still emits Initialized(1); thus after initialization, the getter for _initialized must return 1 for the reference and will return 2 for the mutant.

After a successful initialize(address) call, the contract correctly reports _getInitializedVersion() == 1; the mutant incorrectly sets _initialized = 2, so _getInitializedVersion() returns 2 instead of 1.

After exactly one successful `initialize` call, `_getInitializedVersion()` returns the version that was emitted in the `Initialized` event, which must match the version stored; the mutant emits `Initialized(1)` but stores 2, so the emitted version differs from the stored version.
The initialize function must not revert when called as the first initialization on an uninitialized contract; the bug causes a revert by breaking the construction-phase check.
A first-time call to initialize() on a freshly deployed C must not revert; the bug breaks the construction-phase check and reverts with InvalidInitialization.

A first-time call to initialize with any non-zero address must succeed and set the accessControl; the mutant reverts with InvalidInitialization because the construction check 'initialized == 2' is false for a fresh deployment.

A first-time call to initialize() by anyone on a freshly deployed C must succeed; the mutant M incorrectly treats a pristine deployment as non-constructor initialization and reverts with InvalidInitialization.

After a successful first-time call to initialize(address), the contract's accessControl must be set to the given address; the buggy version reverts with InvalidInitialization because it checks initialized == 2 instead of 1, preventing the accessControl from ever being set.
A call to initialize() should succeed when the contract is uninitialized (initialized == 0), but the mutant incorrectly rejects this initial call.
After a successful call to initialize(address), the contract's initialization state must be 1; the bug causes the call to revert with InvalidInitialization, so initialization never completes.
A call to initialize() should succeed when the contract is uninitialized (initialized == 0), but the mutant incorrectly rejects this initial call.
A call to initialize() must not revert when the contract is uninitialized; the mutant instead reverts because it thinks the contract is already initialized.
A call to initialize() must succeed when the contract is uninitialized; the mutant incorrectly reverts for any address because it requires initialized==1 to attempt initialization.
